content.subject: Electrical Machines
content.hook: Can you extract transformer losses from two simple meter readings?
content.question: A short-circuit test on a transformer gives thirty volts, twenty amperes, and two hundred watts. What is the equivalent resistance?
content.answerLine: The equivalent resistance referred to the metering side is 0.5 ohms.
explanation: In a standard short-circuit test, the secondary winding is bolted short with a thick link.
A small reduced voltage circulates full rated current through the series winding impedances.
Because the applied test voltage is very low, the core flux remains negligibly small.
That means core loss vanishes, so the wattmeter measures pure full-load copper loss.
content.funFact: Open-circuit tests run at rated voltage to find core loss, while short-circuit tests run at rated current to find copper loss!
content.outro: Master both transformer tests to ace your AE and JE exams. Follow for more daily electrical engineering practice!

script.narration: In a standard short-circuit test, the secondary winding is bolted short with a thick link.
A small reduced voltage circulates full rated current through the series winding impedances.
Because the applied test voltage is very low, the core flux remains negligibly small.
That means core loss vanishes, so the wattmeter measures pure full-load copper loss.
Recall that electric power dissipated as heat in a resistor equals current squared times resistance.
Rearranging this basic relation gives resistance as power divided by current squared directly.
Substituting two hundred watts divided by twenty amperes squared gives two hundred over four hundred.
Two hundred divided by four hundred simplifies straight away to zero point five ohms.
Dividing voltage by current would give total impedance, which is one point five ohms instead.
